opus-5.5.text:
I think worst-case complexity is one of the most misapplied ideas when people reason about what neural networks can and can't do. When someone says "Go is PSPACE-hard" or "protein folding is NP-hard," that's a statement about the hardest possible instances in an infinite family of problems: arbitrarily large boards, adversarially constructed energy landscapes. It tells you very little about the instances we actually care about.

Real proteins aren't random sequences. They're the product of billions of years of evolution, which selected for sequences that fold reliably and quickly into stable structures. That's Levinthal's paradox in reverse: if nature can fold a protein in milliseconds, the instances nature produces clearly aren't the worst case. They have exploitable structure, and a neural network trained on lots of examples can learn that structure. AlphaFold didn't solve an NP-hard problem in general. It learned the distribution of problems that biology actually generates.

Go is similar. The 19-by-19 game that humans play is one fixed, finite instance. Asymptotic hardness doesn't constrain how well you can play it. What matters is whether there are good heuristics, meaning patterns in board positions that correlate with winning, and it turns out there are plenty. A value network is essentially an amortized, learned heuristic that compresses an enormous amount of search into a single forward pass.

So the way I'd frame it: complexity theory tells you there's no free lunch across all possible inputs, but deep learning is a bet that the inputs we care about live on a tiny, highly structured slice of that space. You trade guarantees for empirical performance on the distribution you see. The real risk isn't hardness. It's distribution shift. If you get pushed into adversarial or out-of-distribution regions, like the adversarial attacks that found weird exploits in superhuman Go engines, that's where the lack of worst-case guarantees comes back to bite you.

The practical lesson for researchers is to stop asking "is this problem hard?" and start asking "is the data-generating process for this problem structured, and do I have enough of it?" If the answer is yes, a sufficiently expressive model plus search can often go much further than the theory would naively suggest.

r001.rationale: It explains that NP-hardness concerns the hardest possible instances in an infinite problem family and says this tells little about instances encountered in practice.

r002.rationale: It says naturally occurring proteins and human Go positions have exploitable structure that learned models can use.

r003.rationale: It describes a Go value network as a learned heuristic that compresses search and says practical play does not require solving the problem exactly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think worst-case complexity is mostly the wrong lens for this, and the fact that we keep reaching for it tells you something about how computer scientists were trained rather than about how the world actually works.

Here's the way I'd frame it. When someone says Go is hard, or protein folding is NP-hard, what they're really saying is: there exists a family of adversarially constructed instances where no polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee the optimal answer. That's a true statement. But it's a statement about the worst instance in an enormous space, and the instances we actually care about are not sampled from that adversarial distribution. Real proteins are the output of evolution. They're the ones that fold reliably in milliseconds inside a cell, because the ones that didn't fold got selected out. So the distribution of proteins that exist in biology is, almost by construction, a distribution of easy-ish instances. Levinthal's paradox was never really a paradox for nature, and I think AlphaFold is in some sense exploiting the same fact. It's learning the structure of the distribution, not solving the general problem.

Go is similar. A 19x19 board has a combinatorial game tree that is astronomically large, but the positions that arise from two strong players is a tiny, highly structured manifold inside that space. AlphaGo didn't beat Lee Sedol by searching the game tree. It beat him by having a very good prior over which moves are plausible, and then doing a modest amount of search on top. The learned value function is an amortized solution to a problem that would be intractable to solve from scratch each time.

So the takeaway I'd give is: neural networks are fundamentally about average-case performance on a natural data distribution. Worst-case complexity theory is about guarantees that hold even if an adversary picks the input. Those are just different questions. When people say "but neural nets can't solve NP-hard problems," they're correct in the sense that there will always be instances where the network gets it wrong. But that's also true of humans, of heuristics, of basically every practical solver we've ever built. The interesting question isn't whether the worst case is hard. It's whether the data distribution you actually face has enough regularity that a function approximator can learn to exploit it.

Where I think worst-case thinking does still matter is in the failure modes. If you deploy a learned solver in a setting where someone can choose the inputs, like security, or a game-theoretic setting where your opponent is also learning, then you've effectively moved yourself back toward the adversarial distribution. And you'll see that the network falls apart in ways that a classical algorithm with guarantees wouldn't. That's the right place to be humble about it. But for most of the problems we talk about, protein folding, perception, planning in a kitchen, the inputs come from a world that's indifferent to you rather than hostile to you, and I think that's why this stuff works as well as it does.

r001.rationale: It contrasts adversarial worst-case instances with the natural distributions of instances encountered in practice.

r002.rationale: It describes real proteins as shaped by evolution and Go positions from strong play as a small, highly structured subset of all possibilities.

r003.rationale: It says AlphaGo used learned move priors and modest search, making clear a neural approach can succeed in Go without solving for an exact optimum.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between solving every possible instance of a problem and solving the distribution of instances you actually care about. Worst-case complexity constrains the first claim. It doesn’t necessarily tell you very much about the second.

You can have a problem that’s intractable in the worst case, but where the instances that occur in nature have a lot of structure. A neural network can learn to exploit that structure. With proteins, for example, predicting the structures of naturally occurring sequences is a different task from finding the minimum-energy configuration of every arbitrary sequence under some mathematical model. And predicting a structure isn’t the same as simulating the folding process.

Go has a similar distinction, although its precise complexity classification depends on how you generalize the game. Being extraordinarily good at playing Go doesn’t mean you can compute the optimal move in every possible position. You can beat every human while still having blind spots or positions where your search becomes prohibitively expensive.

So I’d take worst-case complexity seriously as a limit on universal guarantees, but not as an argument that learning can’t produce tremendous practical progress. The interesting question is: what structure is the model exploiting, how widely does that structure hold, and what happens when you encounter an instance where it breaks down?

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes worst-case intractability from the structured instances that arise in practice and says worst-case complexity limits universal guarantees, not practical progress.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes structure in naturally occurring protein instances, but does not clearly say that practically relevant Go instances, or both problem types generally, typically have substantial structure.

r003.rationale: It says a system can be extraordinarily good at Go—even beating every human—without computing the optimal move in every possible position.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish solving the worst case from solving the distribution of problems you actually care about. An NP-hardness result says that there are instances that are hard; it doesn’t say that the instances you encounter in nature, or in a game played by humans, are all equally hard.

Take Go. The generalized problem can be computationally intractable, but that doesn’t prevent a neural network from learning an incredibly useful policy and value function for the positions that arise in actual play. You don’t need to exhaust the game tree to play better than any human. You need good intuitions about which branches are worth exploring.

Protein folding has a similar distinction, though the computational problem depends on exactly how you formulate it. Predicting the structures of naturally occurring proteins is different from finding the minimum-energy configuration of every arbitrary amino acid sequence under some model. Evolution has selected a very particular distribution of proteins, and that distribution has structure you can learn.

So worst-case complexity is a constraint on what we should claim: these systems haven’t made computational hardness disappear. But it’s not necessarily a good predictor of their practical usefulness. The interesting question is how much structure there is in the problems we care about, and how effectively learning can exploit it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes hard worst-case instances from the distribution of instances encountered in nature or actual play.

r002.rationale: It says naturally occurring proteins have a learnable distributional structure and points to exploitable structure in the problems encountered in practice.

r003.rationale: It says a neural policy and value function can improve Go play without exhaustively searching the game tree or finding an exact optimum.
